explanation: Fires on interior or continuation subword tokens of multi-token technical, mostly biomedical or chemical compound terms (paraff-in-embedded, sodium dodecyl sulfate, glomer-ular, plasmin-ogen, metal-oxide-sem-iconductor, end-stage). The strongest firing is on a middle piece of a long fixed scientific phrase. Ordinary words in non-technical text give only weak, scattered firing.

Fires strongly on a wide spread of unrelated tokens: adverbs like strictly, purely and vaguely, the prefix non- in noncancerous, anatomical pieces like cytoplasm, corpus and spinal cord, code tokens like .length and charset, and 'aged'. No shared feature is visible across them.

Fires on 'to' in the patent boilerplate 'The (present) invention/disclosure relates (generally) to', at near-max for every such case. It fires more weakly on other words of patent-style descriptions (method of, comprises, U.S. Pat.). Outside patent text it is close to zero.

Fires on a token inside a structured identifier or compound name where the earlier context already fixes the continuation, e.g. the '.' or suffix in repeated citation keys (@pbio.1002..., @pgen), version strings, file names (dvb_demux.h), code identifiers (myCtrl), and fixed medical term endings (saphen-ous, frontotemp-oral). Firing is strongest on predictable continuations of an identifier that was seen before.

Fires on the first token of a new sentence or statement after a boundary such as a header, a blank line or the end of the previous statement. Typical cases are 'I' at the start of the body of a Q&A post or blog, 'if' after a blank line in a script, and the first token after 'v.' or 'No.' in legal captions. Mid-sentence tokens are weak.

Fires on a token within formulaic boilerplate where the continuation is fixed by convention: 'Appeal [from] the United States District Court' in legal captions, 'to [COM] components' in AssemblyInfo, '.m' in Objective-C file headers, 'Inc.,' and commas in addresses and license text, 'get; [set];'. It responds to near-deterministic tokens in templated document headers. Free prose is weak.

Fires on tokens in highly formulaic or templated text: software license boilerplate (conditions are [met], copyright [notice], [distribution], [documentation]), Java override methods (equals, toString), 'Case: 1...' headers, and random base64 strings. It also fires on scattered prose words like measuring and insight, so it is a mixture centred on boilerplate.

Fires mostly on ordinary function words and common tokens in non-English text (Czech, German, Dutch, Danish, Norwegian, Portuguese, Chinese), and also on function words in some English sentences ('By [the]', 'do [not]', 'never [really]'). It seems to track multilingual or generic mid-sentence tokens, but the English cases make the pattern loose.

Fires on the word-initial subword 'pro' or 'prof' and its variants (Pro, prof, prov, proph, prost) at the start of a multi-token word: profuse, prophylaxis, profiling, Profits, Pro Bowl, Protesters, prosthesis. Whole-word tokens that begin with pro-, such as profile, proportion and program, fire weaker.

Fires on 'of' in court names in legal case captions ('Supreme Court [of] Oklahoma', 'Court of Appeals [of] Texas', 'COURT OF CRIMINAL APPEALS [OF] TEXAS'). It is moderate on nearby caption and citation tokens, such as years in citations, 'Appeal from the [United]' and 'appeals [to]'. Elsewhere it is weak.

Fires on tokens in stock boilerplate phrases near the start of a document or section: the '-' after a news dateline '(Reuters)', 'Associated [Press]' photo credits, 'Privacy [Policy]', 'Possible [Duplicate]', 'Welcome [to]', 'easy [to]', 'most [recent]', license 'above [copyright]'. These are predictable tokens of stereotyped header or credit phrases.

Fires on two unrelated kinds of token. One is identifiers in C# and Objective-C boilerplate (AssemblyProduct, NSManagedObjectContext, viewDidLoad, Editors). The other is content words in socio-economic news prose (handicapped, crisis, high-income earners, hungry, overseas, deprivation).

Fires on the second or later subword of an organisation or company name, or on a generic word that refers back to a company ('The [automaker]', 'the [company]'): Kel[logg], Oxford [Instruments], Amicus Ther[apeutics], K[ering], LA[USD]. It is weaker on other proper-name continuations and on unrelated domain nouns.

Fires on words for the people served by an organisation, or on what they experience, in service or mission-statement language: 'improve your [experience]', 'support for [patients]', 'harms [consumers]', 'many [people]', 'you', 'total [satisfaction]', 'survivors'. It is strongest on cookie and customer-service boilerplate.

Fires most clearly on 'respectively' at the end of a list of numbers in scientific text. It also fires strongly on scattered unrelated tokens: idioms ('So far [so] good', 'in [question]', 'A friend [of] mine'), 'should [have]', 'Fentanyl', 'Comparable' and 'amicus'.

Fires on tokens of many unrelated kinds: the opening '(' before birth dates in biography leads ('Jake Jones [(]'), the markdown '*' for emphasis, medical adjectives (vaginal, endotracheal), pronouns like it and you, and code tokens like 'null'. No single theme is visible.

Fires on a heterogeneous set of tokens: phrase completions ('move [on]', 'So far [so]', 'piece [of]'), subword continuations (JSF[iddle], Str[ain], dis[son]ance, Minim[ally]), whitespace runs and code tokens. There is no coherent shared property.

Fires mainly on 'how' or 'way' after expressions of uncertainty or of not knowing ('not sure [how]', 'haven't found a [way]', 'how does it work'). It also fires on the first content token of a name or identifier after a title or label (func [warn], Is [Jay] Z, the [Pen]zCraft, a [android]StoreApp).

Fires on headings, labels or keys in structured or form-like text, typically right after a line break: 'Images[:]', 'Shipping [Information]', 'Mobile', 'Telephone', 'Screens[hots]', JSON keys like 'stringArray', '@version'. It also fires on name continuations (Barrow[man], Shand[ong]).

Fires on the first subword of a word that is split into several tokens, especially lowercase onsets such as lo-oting, rep-atriated, rep-ulsive, ap-athetic, n-oshed and capitals like P-roud or AP-PELLATE. It also fires on function words in Portuguese, Spanish and Hungarian text. The token is the first fragment of a word that continues.

Fires on tokens that complete a technical or product name or a fixed term, without a clear unifying theme: Lin[otype], Pdf[Reader], Pri[us], STM[3]2, X[Namespace], Accept[-Encoding], CSS values (wrap, auto), die[-cut]. It is loosely about the second part of technical compound names, but the examples are mixed.
